blocks.x: Now, I want you to look at this here.
Well this is all good.
It took me two years before I got it. That's your baptismal?
Now, this is from the health department.
Oh, that's your birth certificate.

Yeah. You were born in? See, I was born in March, 1888, but they got me 1888. They got me born in May, 2nd of May. 2nd of May, 1889. Yeah, 1889. And you were born March the what? 1888, March the 7th. But the people got, I mean the place got burnt, you know what I mean?
Oh, I see.
Where were you born? Well, see, I got to go by this now, you see. Yeah, you better go by that. That's what I'm saying, you see, yeah, that'd be the best, you know. Your father's name was? Freo.
Freo, I remember.
Poverisher, yeah.
How's that spelled?
F-E-R-E-O-L, and Papa Joe just like he spelled it. Freo Poverisher. And your mother was Alice?
Alice Poverisher. Alice Poverisher. Alice Poverisher.
Alice Poverisher, mm-hmm. She was P-H-R-L-L-R-P-P-E.
That's it.
Mm-hmm. Did your father play music?

My father used to play the carnage. Oh. Yeah, but my father was most, then from a carnage he was a seagull maker, you know what I mean, in New Orleans, you see. And then he took a fishing pole and made a flute out of it, it blew.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah, my father started out. And my father died of the age of, in 1933, I believe it was November the 13th.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah, I was in Columbia, me and my wife.
You were where?
Columbia, me and my wife, that's my wife's home. And my poor dad, yeah, you know what I mean?
And what was he like? Was he what you'd call a classic type musician, or a musician, or would you call him a ragtime player?

Who was that, my father? Yes. No, he used to play with the boys around there for a good time, you know what I mean, around there. He didn't ever like no bands. But he used to go around with them boys, like break day, but sometimes it was two o'clock in the morning, one o'clock in the morning, and nothing you'd do and surprise you. And you'd be your birthday, and your wife wouldn't tell you nothing, you know? And then you'd be sleeping, your wife's all around, everybody knocking the bomb bomb. And the time your wife opened the door, he might open the door, that's what I play after the birthday for me. That's what I'm surprised to me, you understand? That's why it goes.
Do you remember any of the tunes he played other than Happy Birthday?
Well no, it's been some years back, you know. I forgot, it might be after the birthday, it always was there, you know what I mean?
Yeah, see.

Oh, I don't know. And that's why my cousin, his name's Auguste, Auguste's name, Auguste is French, but he was playing in 28, playing bass. Was his name Pavageo? No, it was my mother's sister's son, the oldest son, yeah, Auguste's name was, you see. He used to play in 28, he used to play guitar and bass. And then he had a room in the back, but he wouldn't give his mama the key, I used to go up there clean, but he had his guitar to tune him, that's why I learned myself to play guitar.
Oh yeah.

Yeah, nobody should play guitar in any of that bass. What was his last name, do you remember? His name was, it was, Auguste, Auguste's name was, you see, yeah. I believe his name was Auguste Phillip, I believe his name was, I believe it is, Auguste Phillip, yeah. And from there when I stole, the one day, I believe it was on a Sunday night, they had a supper home, and it was boys coming down and playing, and my boys playing, and they would take a fishing pool and make a flute I was playing, and my cousin Auguste was playing bass. My other cousin, Fennel, was playing guitar. The other fella called Fortunet, was playing violin, and my cousin made the wrong chord on the guitar. And I told him, my cousin Auguste, I said, you're doing what I said, you made the wrong key. I said, my cousin Fennel, they made the right chord. He said, how do you know? He said, you can play as a show. And my mom and my little sister was small, you know, and I was about 14, 15 years old. I grabbed the guitar. I said, play a same piece over, and I learned my cousin, he stopped playing. You know the piece? No, that was a mazooka though. Oh. That was a long time ago, it was a mazooka. I said, long time ago. Gene doesn't make sure they got it now, I said, mazooka. And from there they picked me up and they brought me inside and ready to give me a lot of pleasure. And then that time, you know what I mean, I surprised them, you see, and they were satisfied. What kind of dances did they have then? Oh, that time we had mazooka, polka, wall, charlotte, cadre, ping-pong, KC, slow drag, and two of them I really forgot, you know what I mean. What is this ping-pong like? Yeah, ping-pong? Well, it's just a dance, you'll dance around, you know what I mean, like this dance you got there now, but it's a different step. And the charlotte's dance was a nice dance, wall's dance, another dance. By the day you can't get no wall's dance or charlotte's dance, mazooka, polka. You can't find a cakewalk, made I don't think. You got to have a cup, you see. You read it, I'm telling you, it was a nice dance that time, I see. Because I used to fire Maine Perez in there, and then that Maine Perez band, they had Gold Rule band, and then they had Butter Bowling band. I used to fire them, you see. Yeah, that was a good time that time.
Well, did you know any of the guys in these different bands? Did you know people in Perez's and the Golden Rule and Bowling?

You know any of the other men? Yeah, I don't know any of the other bands. Yeah, I don't know any of the other bands. It was Maine Perez, Alphonse Pico. There was Billy Murray at bass, Jimmy Fallon's violin, and they had this Mick Murray on the drum. Tramborne was, let me try to get this number just to make it straight, Phil. The name was Phil. And that's my first wife, my first wife's cousin, Phil.
Was he related to George Phil? I don't know.
What did he play? Tramborne, Big Phil.
Well that's who it was, wasn't it George? I guess. I was trying to find out. Yeah. What was it in George? And now who was in the Golden Rule? Adolph and Boo Boo.

What did Adolph? Adolph was playing cornet. He was a shoemaker, playing cornet, he was playing trumpet. And Boo Boo was playing slide, playing tramborne, very tramborne. That time they didn't use a slide tramborne again now. And they had this father called, let me just play guitar, I believe it was, not going to San Diego, no, it was, it had been some long, you know. I think it was Ramon Quay. Ramon? Ramon Quay. No, you don't know him. He wasn't born yet. I was about 17, 16, 17 years old, talking about something. What was his last name? Ramon Quay. He was a brother by Chukka. And he had his hair, no, he had his hair, no, he had his hair, no, he had his hair, no, he had his hair. He had his hair, no, he had his hair, no, he had his hair. And he had his hair, nice hair, and he'd be drunk and be playing guitar. And he'd never make a mistake. Did he look like me or something? I mean, your color, I mean, he had nice straight hair. Yeah, that's all I was. He was guitar playing. Yeah, he was a guitar, I mean, cop, like where the San Diego, where I wasn't compared with him at all. No? And Joe Brooks, I know all of them. Joe Brooks? Joe Brooks. Who did he play with? Man Joe, Mani Perez. Mani Perez changed his name, the Imperium band changed his name three times. The first name was Boys and Blues. It was the first band that came out with a uniform. And then it came to be the Superm band. And then the last that had the Imperium band, you see, changed his name three times. That's Mani Perez's band.
Back to this golden rule, this Adolph who played cornet, did he have a son who played or anything?
Not to my nose.
I was wondering if that was Adolph Alexander's father. I don't know.
I know Fede Keppett and Louis Keppett. Oh? Yeah. See, they had a band too, you see.
What was it called?

What I don't know, I believe they had a makeup band, you know what I mean? Yeah, Tehran. Fede Keppett was playing trumpet, Louis Keppett playing guitar. We used to want to tell them to the same people, when the band told them to his guitar down and rip the bit.
I never heard that. That's Louis Keppett, didn't you?

Louis Keppett, yeah. He was the one coming there, he was the first one who took a piece of sandpaper, he was playing guitar, and when they come to each party, he put the guitar down and take the sandpaper. That's why the sandpaper job got right behind me. Well that's enough, I'm tired now. I can't even think about more. Say. Oh yeah, but my bass. Now the bass I had, when I made, when I took a soapbox and put twine around it. And on a Monday was the Blue Monday, and people around there thought I used to laugh at me. You can laugh all you want, but I know what I'm doing. About me playing guitar, sure, Joseph Davis had to play guitar, while we had Piku singing, and he's the one who composed by Eh La Ba. Piku? Yeah, I knew this Piku. I'm talking about his brother. Alphonse's brother. Yeah, his brother. But she didn't see, Eh La Ba don't go like that. Mm-hmm. You know what this? Just like wife and husband be fussing. Mm-hmm. And she tell you, she tell you, you didn't tell me to go there. And she said, yeah, she told me. No, no, you didn't tell me. Yes, I told you. You know what I mean? It's fussing, see? That's where Eh La Ba go, see? It was like a Mardi Gras song, on a Mardi Gras day. Mm-hmm. And then after I learned, and I went and I heard the boss, I believe it was Bill Morell. That's what it was the whole song. So they're shooting up, boy. He's shooting up, Bill Morell, and I said, give me an A string. I took a pencil, I put an A.
You took a pencil?
Yeah, mark A.
Marked it on the box.

Yeah, yeah. So give me a D string. He said, I have a D string. I'm like, I put D. I use G. I put G. I use G. So, he said, I have G. I eat. I eat. Uh-huh. That's all I want, you know. And I thought I'd go to dance. Well, like, on a Monday, it was a Blue Monday. Well, Raps and Slane, they call me, she stayed in the shallots. And then, boom, on the ground, then, there, beer, and all that stuff, chick, get cooked. So, I turned around, I took the toolbox. Twine on it, nothing about twine. But I had a base key on it, you know what I mean? I got from, I got from all, I love the rubber show. Yeah, the whole base was all broke, and I was washing, you know. He used to like wine. See, the base was all broke. I said, I said, it's a man. Oh, ain't no good, I'm going to throw away. I said, wait a while, give me that neck here. I said, give me that neck here. I said, all I want is the key. I'll give him fifty cents. For the key on that base, see, that's when I turn around and put it on that piece of it, that's when I need to tighten my string up. Well, I know the A on the guitar, the same thing on the bass. G on the guitar, the same thing on the bass. G on the guitar, the same thing on the bass. So, one of the days we started playing. I didn't, I didn't tune up a tall.
I said, oh, where do you want, brother?

I said, give me A. I told you, I think about that piece of paper in my pocket. Give me A. Boom, boom, boom, boom, quang, quang, that whole string kept on going. The key, you know. I got that tune up, that tune up, my D and my G. I said, I play some more, right? My air is all playing, turn around there. But really, while I was first, then I knew the key. And the old key for me, they make on that bass was B flat. And the same thing you make F or C. When I come to me, I says, then they was playing a piece in 4G. When I was, I said, no, no. I was just playing for guitar. I said, hit your G. I said, oh, you make G, it's a bounce, that's an open string. D is an open string, too. See, it comes to my mind. And that's why I told him I'd come up. And that's why I made that. And from there, when I went by Martin's Ghost on Arlene and Robson, I pick up on those barrels, on them round barrels, upright barrels. Let me with them, with them upright boards. That's why I made that little bass. Oh, out of a barrel.
Yeah, out of a barrel.

And I had that bass for me and my wife, and I showed my wife how to play guitar, too. She can play guitar and play my little bass, too. She can play piano and organ. Well, we used to play the Auto Crack on Fridays and Sunday. Me and my wife and Piku, Julius Piku and St. Paper George, we used to play there on Friday Sunday night. I thought we used to play there.
What happened to Sandpaper George? He'd been there.
He died. He died before, before Julius Piku died. Oh.
Did he play anything except Sandpaper?

That's all, Sandpaper. He couldn't do nothing about Sandpaper. He left one day with Aberglenny. He's dead too. Aberglenny. You were the speaker. I'm from speaker. Joseph Davis and St. Paper George. They went to Berkey. And Aberglenny had his bass. And then I was dancing in the meantime, and when they got to play, and Aberglenny had his bass. And everybody was drinking, and St. Paper George had a glass of wine, and he said, it's a shame. Everybody drink, and that full thing right there, that full energy, give him a drink. And George took a glass of wine and pulled Aberglenny's bass. And Aberglenny, he got hot. He got hot. He got hot. He got hot. He got hot. He got hot. He went before Joseph Davis and the man in Hamburg. That's how fun people could tell you about that. And that's why I told Rob. But I was not there when they told me about it, you know what I mean? Yeah, it was George. Aberglenny would kill George. But that bitch, yeah.
Say, did the Golden Rule Band and the Imperial and Buddy Bolden's bands, and- It was the same at the same time.

Did they sound alike at all, the bands, or would they sound different? Well I'm going to tell you, Mania had what you call a swing band. A swing band? Yeah. And Buddy Bolden had a blues band, more of the blues, you see. It was at a contest at the Globe's Hall one time. Mania and the Buddy Bolden Band. Well that time Big Al Lewis was playing with Mania, you see. And first do you know Buddy Bolden Sharp.
Oh. No, no.

You see Mania? Mania was a tripper player. Buddy Bolden Sharp. He was afraid, huh? He was scared, sure, because Frankie Deucer was playing trambone with Buddy Bolden. Bob Lyon was trying to shoot on Rampard Street, he was a bass player. And that's all I'm going to tell you now. I'm glad you all come meet me and see, and I appreciate that you all, actually I'm going to have a little talk, but I'm not much of a speaker. Oh we like it.
You're a wonderful speaker.
You tell good stories, man. Yes, I do.
But don't forget now, I used to dance. I was going to ask you about the dancing and where you used to dance. Where were these?

Yeah, I mean, I used to dance. I mean, at Economy Hall, Hope's Hall, Globes Hall, Masonic Hall, New Hall, Funzami Hall. I didn't bother nobody. Didn't bother from a zooka pool, no. But I used to dance more, I used to dance more, I'd get my kicks out of it, and slow drag dance. And about me dance slow drag dance, and they kept on saying, I love slow drag, the dance. Well, they kept that name called me slow drag, you see, and that's when they kept that name. Yeah, I used to have a nice time. Well, let the Lord bless you, and I'm glad you all come see me.
I was going to ask a little bit more, if you have time, about the slow drag. Did you dance that with just one girl, or did you go around in a circle?

One girl, one girl, see, everybody got to have a couple, I mean a couple, see. Just like you would have a lady, you would have a lady with your dancing. And the one with the dance that slow drag the bass, we won the prize. You know, that's when my prize got soon. He used to be a good dancer too. We had a ball called 88, he wanted to throw around and show me that he beat me dancing. I was working painting, I stuck a piece of pine wood in my foot, it must have been about two weeks. A piece of what? Pound wood, I mean, yeah, coming out the leather, you know what I mean, you're sticking out. Litter. And my brother over there and got soon one to us, we're going to catch this. He said, uh-uh, uh-uh, ain't got nothing to do with this. I'm going to win this bet and give me the money or you got to shove it down. So I went and told him, my mother took a piece of rag and took a needle. I told him about me poor, the whole wood come out, but a piece broke in there. About five days or six days after, she'd never even talk. And my mother told me, I said, my mother couldn't walk on that. My mother turned on that and pet me, my sister pet me, and she don't let me even let that stuff come out and she squeezed it. And I passed away for a while, I mean, got weak, you know. Two to about a day and a half after, I turned on that. The more I walk on, I feel better, you know. When I kept on walking, I felt good, you know. So my brother, I said, look, let that go of him. I said, I got him. I said, I got as soon as to let it go. I said, one thing I want you to do. I said, what? I just want me and my lady is going to be here. I want you to take a chalk and mark it right down there. Well, him and his lady right there, I'm going to just take a chalk and mark it down. When the band start, he's going to be in front, I'll be in front. But when the band start, when the band stop, I'm going to start just where that chalk is. Now, if you stop, that would be a door, but you see. Now, if you stop, if I stop, I mean, pass my mark, chalk, and you stop there, and make me, and the first thing in the band, I saw a fool, and I know the time. I know when the band going to stop, and I know a fool. Then I turn around there, and I see where I go, and I slide down, and I turn it around the bench, and I turn it around the bench, and I like doing a chalk, right, chalk? You think chalk like this, where over there? I see. Cheap pop, what you think the bed was? How much? Fifteen dollars. Oh, I know. And the man went nothing, but the bed was on the outside. The lady, the lady get the umbrella. Every team thought I'd win the best, I mean, you don't get nothing.
The lady gets nothing.
The umbrella was the prize. Yeah, the lady gets that, you don't get that.
So you got your fifteen dollars.
Yeah, that's it. And then I believe after that, that'd be that boy, about two, three, we got that boy, and drop himself in the old basin.
He did what?
Drown himself in the basin. Oh. And his name was A.D., the name was called him A.D.
Drowned himself?

In the basin, the old basin there, right there. Yeah, right. That basin street. Yeah, he used to call it a long time ago, a Crown Lake War. Now they call it a lot of people, but it used to be Crown Lake War.
I was going to ask you about Esau McGee and the Undertaker band. Who's Esau McGee? Esau McGee?
The Undertaker band?
I thought you were the one that told me about that a long time ago.

Esau McGee used to play banjo and guitar. What's his name? Esau McGee used to play guitar and banjo. Him and I used to play together. Well I didn't belong to the unit down there. We used to go around, you know, play around in the ballroom, different places, go and pick a collection.
And he would play the banjo, he was the banjo?

Banjo and guitar and bass player too. And what would you play? Well see he was playing, when he was playing banjo I was playing the bass. Sometimes he played banjo, I played the guitar. That's because sometimes it would be three or four, go to that ballroom, like Corn Eyre and Bambam. I mean, you're up in the Corn Eyre, all three them places, go all through that. All the way up on the, to that avenue, around there, and that big ballroom, I thought I would go up in there and pick up a collection. Sometimes we'd pick up six dollars a piece, a collection. That was big money, you know. But at that time he was getting the car, electric cars, with your bass. But now you can't get any more electric cars now, you got to have a cab somewhere, yes, yes indeed.
Did you ever have to carry your bass through a job? No, indeed.
I walked around some close distance, I was up there, I had to go get a license for my bass to get in the car. He charged you nothing free.
Didn't charge you extra for the bass?

No, I mean, you can get the car with your bass, but he didn't charge you nothing free. But no, it's different. I need no more color. Canadi Oakland Canalville . Well, you had buses now. Yeah, buses . And we was playing at . on Sun Rock.
Benefit and Sun Rock?

Yeah, you remember that? Oh yeah. Yeah. I used to catch the electric car in my bass. See, at the time, at the time we was playing the electric car in my bass, and jumped down one corner, I had to walk a block in half to the bass, see?
That's where your bass was in the flood too, wasn't it?
Yeah, I did eight days to the non-end, and the same bass there. I had it down like this, yeah. They were all that high over it.
Well, they went up about four feet, I think, or three feet, anyway.

Yeah, and Lawrence Morello, he had his N-to-five, and his guitar, yeah. Couldn't get down there, take eight days to it. After I go down there, I told my wife, I said, oh baby, what you worried about? I said, oh my, you're seven half-throw instrument. Oh, I went down there, I was sweeping the water. When I took that, same cover I got there, when I went down and took the cover off, and it was in the head and the neck come clean off my hand.
Yeah. What year was that?

Well, let me see what you had done. That wasn't so long ago. You see, 19, that's before in New York, no, after we come from New York. 1847, I think. I think it was, yeah, 1947, yeah, I think it was 1947. And I come in, and the North Shore showed me a place where I couldn't fix that place. And we had to play the St. Joseph Knight. And it was about five days or six days for the St. Joseph Knight. So you need iron clamp. I said, I don't need iron clamp, I know what to do then. I took my wood, make my iron clamp on it. You see, that's my base. So I took a piece of wood like this, and cut it out like this, great. And this leaf, and then I put the piece of wood in, put the plug in it, make it tight. I made about six wood wood.
Well, I think I would drag you, what other jobs have you done? Slater, different things you used to tell me, what other jobs?

Oh, yeah, I used to work, first I used to work for Al Mastricht, 919 on Lobster Street, and I used to do all the slater work, paper hanging, plaster, that's my tray, and I knew that I'd do carbonate work. And I done all that. I went for D'Alandino real estate at 729 Newton Street. I done all that for D'Alandino real estate. And now I went for Miss Ducco at 1301 Barrett Street. She's dead, and her sister died, and all of them cats are from Miss Ducco. My father and neighbors, my parents used to be at a bigger shop. I did some hard work. I got steamboat tour number one, tour number two, on that river, doing all that kind of work. That's why I tell everybody, I don't worry about the work. The work don't kill me. It's just how you do it. I steamboat tour number one, tour number two. And that time you had to be a man. That is all out of the machine. That time you had to pick up. Go to the side of Captain John, on the other side of Captain Zinno, I believe, on the other side. They had to tour. Four men, two men in front, two men in the back, with 400 pounds of ice. 400 pounds of ice? Yeah, it's around here. I don't use cake. Yeah, I don't know that. I took coffee.
Well, can you tell me, once in New York, when you and George were up there, you told me how you used to throw the big bags of coffee up, they had some sort of a little call? Yeah, yeah, sure, but...

Did it in rhythm, or how did you do that? Yes, indeed. Well, see, that time, everything you had to do was pick up. See, one man on the other side of the man there, see? Now, after so much higher, you had to throw it. You already got a little slack. You threw up there, that man put it, and then it went straight up.
Did you sing when you did it? Did you sing or anything, or make any noise, when you would throw that?

No, sometimes you would have to hang, you know, play that thing. When I left, when I come down here, I was, I believe it was 1957, 1958, I worked on a sugar boat there, I was a sweeper. They wouldn't give me a job in the car, because I was too old, you know what I'm saying? My boy would come and go up there, I was a sweeper. When I was getting a dollar car, and they make 14 cars, that's $14 to make. When they used to, they make some cars sometimes, 10, 12 cars, 14, 15 cars, nothing they make on the side of the river, when I was a sweeper. I was a sweeper, that's the last job I'd done in the river.
One other thing I was going to ask about the part of town where you were born, where you were raised. Born in New Orleans. Which part of town, which street?

Well I was born on a way of in between, in the Gulf of the Gulf, in Seven Wall. Used to call Longtown, Good Children's Street. Longtown Good, Good Children's Street, it's Boivy Street. And that's, Good Children's Street, that's where I was born then. People turned around when I was, and I got baptized at the Catella Street. And Pat Meejo, Christian man, he's dead. St. Louis Cathedral?
Yeah, very charitable.

She used to make catechism school, white and colored at times. See, these nine, you know what I'm saying? And catechism, and take communion and everything. Then I used to go to the sister on Alley Street, called the mother of the sister, called Set-by-Morch. She's dead, there'd be some years back. And I used to go there with my oldest brother, called Joseph Piper, sometimes ring that bell. You know, children used to be double, and they'd ring the bell and run. So I run, I done it one day, and the sister come out of it. But one day when I done it, an ass man was coming. And I didn't see him, he grabbed me and brought me brother's sister. He brought me back there, make me go to my knees. I'll never forget all of them. My brother and I, make me go to my knees. My brother, no, that's he down there. But then I was, I was, ooh, I mean, they put him on my knees, they turn around, and tell my mom, my mom, my mom, you know, we're going to do it. From that day in the morning. Yeah, that, see that's why I said I was, I was born, I know, my father and mother told me I was born in 1888, March to seven. But the Christian paper, they had a fire in there about 50 some more years on that side. But I just figured everything there, the book must have been destroyed from the fire, you see. Well, that's the only cop I got. See? See that, it's 18, 18, 1889, ain't it?
Yeah, May the 2nd then, that's where they got on there, see? That's where they got on there, see? Well, I'm going about this now.
Well, Drag, can you tell me, did you ever get uptown when you were young to go to dances, like up at the Masonic Hall or any place uptown? I've been all uptown.

I've been all to Masonic, Globesaw, and New Hall and all them places, downtown, I've been all over. I wonder if you ever went uptown and heard the dances up there too, danced up there. Yeah, like there's a place called, what used to call, it's been on Frankie Street. On Frankie Street, on Frankie Street, let me see, it was, it's called, a lot of times ago, but it's called, I used to call that name. Yes, well, I know the one you mean. The Funky Butthole. The Funky Butthole. The Funky Butthole, on Perdido. Perdido Street, yeah, between the ramparts and the side too, I used to go all the whole time. It used to have nothing but posters.
Was the dancing any different up there than downtown in Deconomy Hall?

Oh yeah, the way you ever see, but the people on that dance, more, it used to be more butter bone playing, bands playing down there, and what, I mean, Ferry Capon used to play like that, nothing but the blues.
You see?

And more to get the blues for, that was butter bone playing, was to play the blues. You see? That's what I told you about, I told you about butter bone, you see, that the people on the play. So one day, before we put it out, they had a, at the gloves hall, at the gloves hall, labor day. So me and my friend went up there and turned around and there was two ladies, two or three ladies was fighting, at the gloves hall. And butter bone's band was on the music stand. Music, music, music. One of them was terrified and I told her I was on the floor, I go ahead, grab some money, put it in my pocket, you know what you're saying? One of them told her I was like, come out that big bunch of, what do you call that big pocket of a watch, you know what I mean? Hit me with one another, put the money. Then I went on the music stand. Hit me with my bass and go to him and I said, get him the bass, and he took the bass and turned around and I go around, somebody showed a bar and cut him right here. Cut him right on the forehead. I told him I hand me his bass, and I never forget the gloves on. Who was that guy? I do, somebody showed a bar. Yeah, but I mean who was the guy that fell? The bass player, I mean he was by a line. segments.title: Birth certificate and parents' names
segments.summary: Pavageau and the visitors look at his birth certificate; he says he was born in March 1888 but the record says 2 May 1889 because the place burned. His parents' names are spelled out.

segments.title: His father's music-making
segments.summary: His father made and played a homemade flute, played informally with friends and serenaded birthdays; Pavageau was in Columbia when his father died in 1933.

segments.title: Cousin Auguste, teaching himself guitar, early dances
segments.summary: He learned guitar on his cousin Auguste's instrument, then corrected a wrong chord at a family supper at age 14-15 and was brought in to play. The same long answer lists the dances of the time and his firing for the Perez, Golden Rule and Bowling bands.

segments.title: Members of the Perez and Golden Rule bands
segments.summary: He names men in Manuel Perez's band and the Golden Rule band, a guitarist Ramon Quay, and how Perez's band changed its name three times.

segments.title: The Keppard brothers and sandpaper guitar
segments.summary: Asked about Adolph's son, he turns to Freddie and Louis Keppard's band, Louis being the first to play sandpaper after guitar at parties.

segments.title: Building his first bass from a soapbox and barrel
segments.summary: He recounts making a bass from a soapbox with twine, marking strings in pencil, getting a tuning key, and later building one from a barrel.

segments.title: Playing with his wife, Piku and Sandpaper George
segments.summary: He played Friday and Sunday nights at the Auto Crack with his wife, Julius Piku and Sandpaper George, and tells of George's quarrel over a bass.

segments.title: Perez versus Buddy Bolden's band
segments.summary: He contrasts Perez's swing band with Bolden's blues band, recalls a contest at Globe Hall, and names Bolden's trombonist and bass player.

segments.title: Dance halls and winning the slow drag contest
segments.summary: He lists the halls where he danced, explains how he got the name Slow Drag, and tells of a chalk-mark dance bet won with a hurt foot for a fifteen dollar prize.

segments.title: A drowning in the old basin
segments.summary: A short aside about a young man named A.D. who drowned himself in the old basin on Basin Street.

segments.title: Esau McGee, playing collections and carrying the bass on streetcars
segments.summary: He played banjo, guitar and bass with Esau McGee around ballrooms for collections, took his bass on electric cars, and recalls it surviving a flood.

segments.title: Repairing his flooded bass
segments.summary: After the flood he found the bass damaged and recalls the repair, dated to about 1947, before a St. Joseph's night job.

segments.title: Day jobs: slater, ice, coffee and the sugar boat
segments.summary: He describes work as a slater, plasterer and painter, hauling ice and coffee on the river, and his last job as a sugar-boat sweeper in 1957-58.

segments.title: Birthplace in Longtown and boyhood school mischief
segments.summary: He says he was born in Longtown, was baptized and attended catechism, and recounts being caught ringing a convent bell; birth date again discussed.

segments.title: Uptown dance halls versus downtown
segments.summary: Asked about uptown dances, he names halls and a Perdido Street dance, saying uptown bands played mostly blues.

segments.title: A fight at Globe Hall and a bass player cut
segments.summary: He tells of a Labor Day brawl at Globe Hall with Buddy Bolden's band on stand and a bass player cut on the forehead.

segments.title: Never played with Buddy Bolden
segments.summary: Asked if he played regularly with Buddy Bolden, he says he never did; the recording ends in repetition.
